- OW-WAR-0069 / Q-001 [blocking]: Where does the board live? The numbered approval list can be a terminal view (war board), a view in the Pages app beside the other projections, or both.
  Recommendation: Both, terminal first: war board renders the list and its exact war sign commands; the Pages board is the same data as a read-only view, since a browser cannot sign.
- OW-WAR-0069 / Q-002 [blocking]: May a performing agent ask mid-run, or only before it starts? Mid-run asking needs the performer to wait, which costs wall time; up-front only needs every question foreseen.
  Recommendation: Both: a performer may ask at any time, but only its own stage waits, and if no answer arrives before the stage's wall time the submission requests block with the question id as the blocker.
- OW-WAR-0069 / Q-003 [blocking]: What does a tick on the numbered list actually do? A browser cannot hold your key, so the tick cannot be the signature itself.
  Recommendation: The tick is a keystroke at the workstation: the board prints rows numbered 1..n, each row the exact war sign command, and war sign --all --ssh-sign walks them one dialog at a time.
- OW-WAR-0142 / Q-001 [blocking]: How is routine work authorized? A: a standing authorization. You sign one class (paths, basic assurance, named gates, a budget, an expiry and a count), and each Warrant inside it is authorized from that signature, with its own immutable record naming you. Routine change cost: 0 acts before work, one line in a batched resolution after it. Needs an additive SAS 1.2.0 (§28.8, a clause in §37.5, one §106 row); §27.2 does not change. B: no standing authorization, only batching and presets. Cost: 2 batches per round, and every change waits for your authorize batch before it starts. C: a SAS revision of §27.2 so routine work needs no authorization, with the same per-change cost as A, but the invariant that every authorized Warrant has a human authorizer is dropped. OW-ADR-0029 has the full comparison. Answer A, B or C.
  Recommendation: A. It gives the per-change cost C gives and keeps §27.2 intact: you signed, and the record names you. It extends §30.2's pre-authorization pattern from revisions to new instances. B keeps the wait before work, which is the friction you named.
- OW-WAR-0142 / Q-002 [blocking]: Under A, what bounds does a class carry by default? The draft proposes an expiry of at most 90 days from signing, at most 50 covered Warrants, and a ceiling of 24000 budget_tokens and 1800 wall_time_seconds per stage. Answer with the numbers, or 'as drafted'.
  Recommendation: as drafted: 90 days, 50 Warrants, 24000 tokens and 1800 s per stage. Revoking or re-signing a class is one act, so short bounds are cheap.
- OW-WAR-0142 / Q-003 [blocking]: Under A, may a covered (routine) Warrant take ownership of a path whose current owner is an authorized but unresolved Warrant? OW-ADR-0021 would let the later authorization own it. Answer 'refuse' or 'allow'.
  Recommendation: refuse. Routine work should not silently take a file from work in flight. The in-flight Warrant resolves first, or you sign the routine change individually.
- OW-WAR-0069 / Q-004: May a question be asked with no stage, at program level (a question about the SAS rather than a stage)?
  Recommendation: No. A question with no stage has nothing to unblock and nobody to read it; a program-level question belongs to a decision Warrant's stage (war-map), which is cheap to create.
- OW-WAR-0069 / Q-005: Is the performer configured once per repository, or named per stage?
  Recommendation: Once per repository ([perform] performer_argv), like the drafter and the verifier; the stage's executor_ref names WHICH agent in prose, and a mismatch is a refusal, not a second configuration surface.
- OW-WAR-0069 / Q-006: How many agent stages may run at once under war perform --all?
  Recommendation: One in 1.0 ([perform] max_concurrent = 1). Nothing contains a performer (no cgroups, no sandbox), so concurrency would mean several unbounded processes in one tree; raise it when containment exists.
